questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A study shows a treatment works in one lab but may not apply elsewhere

options.text: This concerns external validity of the finding
This concerns internal validity of the finding
This concerns reliability of the measurement
This concerns statistical power of the test

questions.explanation: External validity concerns whether results generalise to other settings or populations. Internal validity concerns causal inference within the study.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A study reports a significant effect that later proves unstable

options.text: This is only an internal validity problem
Threats to statistical conclusion validity may be present
This is only an external validity problem
This proves the measures are unreliable

questions.explanation: Statistical conclusion validity concerns whether statistical inferences about covariation are accurate. Unstable effects suggest assumption or power problems.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Many participants drop out before the final measurement in a trial

options.text: Attrition proves the intervention failed
Attrition only reduces sample size
Attrition can bias results if dropouts differ from completers
Attrition is harmless with random assignment

questions.explanation: When dropouts differ systematically from those who remain, the final sample may be biased. Random assignment does not prevent differential attrition.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Volunteers for a wellness programme differ in motivation from non-volunteers

options.text: Selection effects are the same as attrition
Volunteering guarantees a representative sample
Selection effects only matter in experiments
Selection effects may explain outcome differences

questions.explanation: Pre-existing differences between those who select into a programme and those who do not can confound its apparent effect.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A workplace event occurs midway through a six-month study

options.text: History effects only matter in cross-sectional studies
The event may confound changes attributed to the intervention
History effects are the same as maturation
A control group cannot reduce history effects

questions.explanation: External events occurring during a study can produce changes mistaken for intervention effects. A control group helps isolate the intervention effect.
questions.hint: What else happened during the study?

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Staff naturally improve at a task over a year of practice

options.text: Maturation is the same as history
Maturation only affects children
Improvement may reflect maturation rather than the intervention
Maturation cannot be controlled in any design

questions.explanation: Natural change over time can mimic an intervention effect. Control groups and time-series designs help separate maturation from treatment effects.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Staff score higher on a second administration of the same test

options.text: Testing effects are the same as maturation
Improvement proves the intervention worked
Testing effects only occur with paper tests
Improvement may reflect practice from prior testing

questions.explanation: Prior exposure to a test can improve scores through practice or familiarity, independent of any intervention.
questions.hint: Has the measure been given before?

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Extremely low performers are selected for a coaching programme and improve

options.text: Improvement proves the coaching works
Improvement may partly reflect regression to the mean
Regression only affects high performers
Regression is the same as maturation

questions.explanation: Extreme scores tend to move toward the average on retest even without intervention, creating apparent improvement.
questions.hint: What happens to extreme scores on retest?

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Staff work harder when they know they are being observed

options.text: Observer effects only occur in laboratories
This proves the workplace is productive
This is an observer effect that can distort behaviour
Observer effects are the same as placebo

questions.explanation: Awareness of observation can change behaviour, known as the Hawthorne effect. Blinding or unobtrusive measures reduce it.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A report runs twenty separate significance tests on the same data

options.text: Families are only for ANOVA designs
Each test has its own independent error rate
Only planned tests form a family
These tests form a family sharing one error budget

questions.explanation: Multiple tests on the same data constitute a family, and their combined chance of a false positive exceeds the per-test rate.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: With twenty tests at alpha 0.05 the chance of at least one false positive rises

options.text: The family-wise rate stays at 0.05
The family-wise error rate exceeds 0.05
The family-wise rate falls with more tests
The family-wise rate depends only on sample size

questions.explanation: As more tests are performed, the probability of at least one false positive increases, so the family-wise error rate exceeds the nominal level.
questions.hint: More tests, more chances for false positives.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A report runs five tests and applies Bonferroni; the adjusted alpha is 0.01
questions.explanation: Dividing 0.05 by five tests gives 0.01. The Bonferroni adjustment keeps the family-wise error rate near 0.05.
questions.hint: Divide 0.05 by the number of tests.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A study reports a standardised mean difference of 0.5

options.text: The effect is statistically significant at 0.05
The groups differ by half a raw score unit
The groups differ by half a standard deviation on average
The effect is negligible because it is below 1

questions.explanation: A standardised mean difference expresses the group difference in standard deviation units, so 0.5 means half a standard deviation.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Two variables share 25 percent of their variation

options.text: Shared variation means one causes the other
Their correlation is 0.25
Their shared variation is 25 raw units
Their correlation squared is 0.25

questions.explanation: The proportion of shared variation is the squared correlation. If r squared is 0.25, then r is 0.5 in absolute value.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A confidence interval becomes wider when sample size shrinks

options.text: Smaller samples yield narrower intervals
Smaller samples yield wider intervals due to more uncertainty
Sample size does not affect interval width
Interval width depends only on the mean

questions.explanation: Smaller samples provide less information, increasing standard error and widening the confidence interval.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Two variables have a covariance of 12 and standard deviations of 3 and 4; the correlation is 1
questions.explanation: Correlation equals covariance divided by the product of standard deviations: 12 divided by 12 equals 1. This indicates a perfect positive linear relationship.
questions.hint: Divide covariance by the product of standard deviations.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Event rates are 0.20 in the treated group and 0.12 in the control group; the risk difference is 0.08
questions.explanation: Risk difference is the treated rate minus the control rate: 0.20 minus 0.12 equals 0.08. This expresses the absolute effect.
questions.hint: Subtract the control rate from the treated rate.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: The same staff are measured before and after a training programme

options.text: Paired comparisons are only for experiments
A paired comparison ignores the pairing
A paired comparison accounts for within-person correlation
Paired comparisons always increase variance

questions.explanation: Paired designs use within-person differences, reducing variability from person-to-person differences. Ignoring pairing wastes information.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A longitudinal report keeps 85 percent of participants over two years

options.text: Retention guarantees no selection bias
Retention is the same as response rate
Retention only matters for qualitative work
High retention reduces attrition bias risk

questions.explanation: Retaining most participants reduces the risk that dropouts bias longitudinal findings. It does not eliminate selection bias at entry.
questions.hint: How many stay in the study?

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Standardised mean difference from a test statistic
questions.learningObjective: Convert a test statistic to an effect size
questions.stem: A t-test with a large sample yields a small p-value but a small mean difference

options.text: A small p-value guarantees a large effect size
The standardised mean difference may still be small
Effect size is irrelevant once p is small
The t-statistic equals the effect size

questions.explanation: Statistical significance reflects sample size and precision, while effect size reflects magnitude. A large sample can make a tiny effect significant.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A report states p equals 0.03 for a workplace intervention

options.text: The effect size is 0.03
There is a 3 percent chance the hypothesis is true
If the null were true, such a result would be unlikely
The result is practically important

questions.explanation: A p-value is the probability of observing data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true. It is not the probability the hypothesis is true.
questions.hint: Assume the null is true first.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A report wants narrower confidence intervals for the same mean

options.text: Ignore variability and use the mean only
Increase the confidence level to 99 percent
Reduce the sample size to focus on key cases
Increase sample size or reduce variability

questions.explanation: Narrower intervals come from more data or less variability. Raising the confidence level or shrinking the sample widens intervals.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why effect sizes accompany tests
questions.stem: A report presents p-values but no effect sizes

options.text: Effect sizes are redundant with p-values
Effect sizes convey magnitude that p-values omit
Effect sizes are only for meta-analysis
Effect sizes replace significance tests

questions.explanation: P-values indicate whether an effect is detectable, while effect sizes indicate how large it is. Both are needed for interpretation.
questions.hint: What does p not tell you?

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An intervention shows a tiny but statistically significant effect

options.text: Practical significance requires a larger p-value
Statistical significance guarantees practical importance
The effect may lack practical significance despite being detectable
Practical significance is the same as effect size

questions.explanation: A result can be statistically detectable yet too small to matter in practice. Context and cost determine practical significance.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A report finds a correlation between office plants and productivity

options.text: The correlation is meaningless without significance
The plants cause higher productivity
The correlation proves no confounds exist
The variables covary, but causation is not established

questions.explanation: Correlation indicates covariation, not causation. Confounds or reverse causality could explain the association.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Ice cream sales and drowning incidents rise together in summer

options.text: Ice cream sales cause drowning
Temperature is a lurking variable affecting both
Drowning causes ice cream sales
The correlation is spurious only if p is large

questions.explanation: A lurking variable such as temperature can create an association between two unrelated outcomes. Controlling for it removes the spurious link.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An observational report claims a training programme caused better performance

options.text: Observation supports causation if p is small
Observation alone supports causation if the sample is large
Causal claims require design features beyond observation
Observation never yields any useful findings

questions.explanation: Observational designs lack random assignment, so confounds may explain the association. Causal claims need stronger design or adjustment.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

options.text: Non-equivalence is fixed by larger samples
Non-equivalent groups are as good as randomised groups
Non-equivalence only affects sample size
Pre-existing differences may confound the comparison

questions.explanation: Without random assignment, groups may differ before treatment, confounding outcomes. Matching or adjustment can help but not fully fix this.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS

options.text: Consent is just signing a form
Informed consent requires disclosure and voluntary agreement
Consent is unnecessary for low-risk surveys
Consent can be implied by participation

questions.explanation: Informed consent involves informing participants of risks and benefits and obtaining voluntary agreement. A signature alone is insufficient.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A workplace study involving staff data needs independent review

options.text: Ethics review is optional for internal reports
Only medical studies need ethics review
An ethics committee reviews risks to participants
Ethics review guarantees no harm

questions.explanation: Ethics review evaluates potential harms and protections for participants, including in workplace research. It reduces but cannot eliminate risk.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: After a study using mild deception participants are told the true purpose

options.text: Debriefing removes all ethical concerns
Debriefing is optional if deception was minor
Debriefing is the same as consent
Debriefing informs participants and mitigates deception

questions.explanation: Debriefing explains the study's purpose and any deception, allowing participants to understand their role. It mitigates but does not erase ethical issues.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A researcher registers hypotheses and analysis plans before collecting data

options.text: Preregistration guarantees correct results
Preregistration reduces selective reporting and p-hacking
Preregistration is only for clinical trials
Preregistration prevents all bias

questions.explanation: Preregistration commits to hypotheses and analyses in advance, reducing selective reporting and p-hacking. It does not guarantee correctness.
questions.hint: What does locking plans in advance prevent?

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A report verifies that participants noticed the intervention condition

options.text: A manipulation check is only for drug trials
A manipulation check replaces the outcome measure
A manipulation check confirms the intervention was received
A manipulation check guarantees the effect

questions.explanation: A manipulation check assesses whether participants experienced the intended condition, supporting internal validity. It does not guarantee an effect.
questions.hint: Did participants experience the intended condition?

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A researcher excludes outliers only after seeing the results

options.text: Only large samples need preregistered exclusions
Post-hoc exclusions are always justified
Exclusions do not affect conclusions
Post-hoc exclusions can bias results and should be preregistered

questions.explanation: Deciding exclusions after seeing data risks cherry-picking. Preregistering exclusion rules protects validity.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A report cites only studies supporting its preferred conclusion

options.text: Selective citation is acceptable if results are strong
Selective citation can bias the apparent evidence base
Selective citation only affects readability
Selective citation is the same as preregistration

questions.explanation: Citing only supporting studies distorts the evidence base and can mislead decision makers. Balanced reviews are needed.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A report paraphrases a finding without citing the original study

options.text: Citation is only for direct quotes
Paraphrasing removes the need for citation
Proper citation credits the original source
Citation is unnecessary for internal reports

questions.explanation: Paraphrased ideas still require citation to credit the original source and allow verification.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS

options.text: Debriefing is the same as consent
Debriefing can be skipped if results are positive
Debriefing is optional after minor deception
Debriefing should explain the deception promptly

questions.explanation: When deception is used, debriefing should occur promptly to explain the true purpose and allow withdrawal of data. Skipping it is unethical.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS

options.text: Historical baselines are as good as randomised controls
Historical comparisons are vulnerable to history and maturation
Historical comparisons eliminate confounds
Historical comparisons are only for qualitative work

questions.explanation: Comparing with a past baseline confounds the intervention with historical events and natural change over time.
questions.hint: What changed between then and now?

questions.topic: Judging an effect against a threshold
questions.learningObjective: Judge an effect against a threshold

options.text: The threshold is irrelevant once p is small
The effect exceeds the threshold because it is significant
The effect falls below the threshold for practical importance
The effect automatically meets any threshold

questions.explanation: Comparing the observed effect with a predefined meaningful threshold shows it falls short of practical importance despite possible significance.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A report shares participant data beyond what was agreed

options.text: This only affects data quality
This is acceptable if names are removed
This is fine for internal reports
This breaks confidentiality and informed consent

questions.explanation: Sharing data beyond agreed terms violates confidentiality and the consent participants gave. De-identification may not fully protect privacy.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A study conducted in one office wants broader applicability

options.text: Increase the sample size in the same office
Replicate in diverse settings and samples
Tighten experimental control further
Use only one outcome measure

questions.explanation: External validity improves through replication across varied settings, populations, and implementations. More of the same office does not broaden applicability.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A study with low power fails to detect a real effect

options.text: Switch to a one-tailed test after seeing data
Lower alpha to 0.01 to improve power
Increase sample size or reduce noise to improve power
Ignore power and rely on p-values

questions.explanation: Power improves with larger samples, less measurement error, or better design. Lowering alpha reduces power, and post-hoc test switching inflates error.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A longitudinal study loses participants over time

options.text: Ignore dropout and analyse completers only
Exclude all dropouts from analysis without checking
Replace dropouts with new participants mid-study
Use incentives and flexible scheduling to retain participants

questions.explanation: Retention strategies such as incentives and flexibility reduce dropout. Simply excluding or ignoring dropouts can bias results.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A programme recruits only highly motivated volunteers

options.text: Volunteering ensures motivated participants only
Random assignment or matching can reduce selection bias
Selection effects are unavoidable in all studies
Increasing sample size removes selection bias

questions.explanation: Random assignment or matching on key variables can reduce selection bias. Sample size does not fix who enters the study.

Ignore the restructuring as irrelevant
Include a control group exposed to the same history
Analyse only post-restructuring data

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS

options.text: Measure outcomes only at the end

Extend the programme to outlast maturation
A control group helps separate maturation from treatment

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS

Use alternate test forms or a control group
Skip the pre-test entirely without reason
Testing effects only matter in education

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods

Attribute all improvement to the intervention
Include a control group of equally extreme scorers
Regression only affects random measurement

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods

Observer effects are harmless in workplace studies
Use unobtrusive measures or blind observers

Multiplicity only matters with small samples
